Compared to existing approaches, an improvement in prediction accuracy of up to 57 % was achieved. Further, we successfully demonstrated the practical applicability of the model within an MPC-based path tracking controller on a real Formula Student race car.

title: LSA: Localized Semantic Alignment for Enhancing Temporal Consistency in Traffic Video Generation
authors: Mirlan Karimov, Teodora Spasojević, Markus Braun, Julian Wiederer, Vasileios Belagiannis, Marc Pollefeys
abstract: Controllable video generation has emerged as a versatile tool for autonomous driving, enabling realistic synthesis of traffic scenarios. However, existing methods depend on control signals at inference time to guide the generative model towards temporally consistent generation of dynamic objects, limiting their utility as scalable and generalizable data engines. In this work, we propose Localized Semantic Alignment (LSA), a simple yet effective framework for fine-tuning pre-trained video generation models. LSA enhances temporal consistency by aligning semantic features between ground-truth and generated video clips. Specifically, we compare the output of an off-the-shelf feature extraction model between the ground-truth and generated video clips localized around dynamic objects inducing a semantic feature consistency loss. We fine-tune the base model by combining this loss with the standard diffusion loss. The model fine-tuned for a single epoch with our novel loss outperforms the baselines in common video generation evaluation metrics. To further test the temporal consistency in generated videos we adapt two additional metrics from object detection task, namely mAP and mIoU. Extensive experiments on nuScenes and KITTI datasets show the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing temporal consistency in video generation without the need for external control signals during inference and any computational overheads. The code is available at https://github.com/mirlanium/LSA

title: A Multi-Modal Driving Dataset with Event-Level Ground Truth for Behavior Evaluation
authors: Bin Guo, John H. L. Hansen
abstract: While smartphone-based driving behavior monitoring offers scalability, its reliability relative to instrumented vehicle measurements remains largely unexplored due to the lack of synchronized ground-truth datasets. This paper presents a synchronized multi-modal naturalistic driving dataset comprising CAN-bus signals, smartphone IMU measurements, GPS trajectories, video recordings, and event-based human annotations collected from 20 drivers over standardized routes totaling over 600 minutes. To enable rigorous cross-modal validation, we develop a principled alignment and scoring framework that synchronizes heterogeneous data streams, extracts robust behavioral features, and calibrates smartphone-derived aggressiveness indices against CAN-bus references through quantile mapping. The resulting 7-level scoring system achieves promising agreement between smartphone and CAN-bus data, demonstrating that properly calibrated smartphones can serve as reliable proxies for vehicle dynamics assessment. This dataset and framework provide the comprehensive resource for evaluating smartphone-based driving behavior sensing against instrumented vehicle ground truth, enabling future research in low-cost, large-scale driver monitoring.

title: TRAP: A Joint Tracking and Prediction Algorithm Towards Unified Perception
authors: Loïc Stratil, Clemens Krispler, Markus Lienkamp
abstract: We present a fully differentiable, joint tracking and prediction model, developed towards unified perception. Our approach, TRAP, is directly leverageable with state-of-the-art 3D object detectors, reformulating the underlying perception tasks into a spatial one, followed by a unified temporal formulation. Specifically, TRAP solves the tracking and prediction tasks within a single algorithm, while retaining standardized and compatible interfaces to upstream detection and downstream planning.Unlike previous joint tracking and prediction approaches, TRAP offers two core advantages. The method is sensor-agnostic, only leveraging 3D bounding box and map information as input, outputting unimodal trajectories for accurate motion prediction. Furthermore, joint tracking and prediction is not naturally capable of predicting the motion of undetected objects, either due to false negatives or occlusion, in a current timestep. To this extent, we propose a novel occlusion propagation module that addresses this limitation. We evaluate TRAP on the nuScenes dataset and show that our joint tracking and prediction approach outperforms its modular baseline. TRAP thereby fortifies the potential of unified perception as an extension to purely modular perception in autonomous driving. https://github.com/TUMFTM/TRAP.

title: An OpenXR-Based Interface for Real-Time Sensor Integration in Intelligent Vehicles
authors: Alexander Kraus, Ansgar R. S. Gerlicher, Christian Hackenbeck
abstract: Extended Reality (XR) technologies—including Virtual, Augmented, and Mixed Reality, are increasingly applied in the automotive domain for design, training, and human–vehicle interaction. However, their integration into vehicle architectures remains fragmented due to proprietary XR runtimes and non-standardized automotive interfaces. This work presents an OpenXR-based interface for integrating real-time sensors in intelligent vehicles. The proposed abstraction model leverages open standards, including OpenXR, Eclipse KUKSA, and the Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS), to enable modular, cross-platform, and interoperable communication between XR devices and vehicle functions. We implemented a prototype using Unity and OpenXR to support bidirectional communication between XR environments and vehicle systems. Two use cases were evaluated: (1) controlling window regulators via XR interaction, and (2) visualizing ultrasonic sensor data in real time. Experimental results demonstrate reliable bidirectional communication, real-time synchronization of sensor data, and stable performance under typical load conditions. Latency measurements confirm the feasibility of the approach, while stress tests reveal scaling limitations under high parallel request loads. The findings high-light the potential of OpenXR and open automotive standards to enable flexible, real-time XR integration in future intelligent vehicle platforms.

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Deep Learning-Based LiDAR Super-Resolution for Autonomous Driving
authors: June Moh Goo, Zichao Zeng, Jan Boehm
abstract: LiDAR sensors are often considered essential for autonomous driving, but high-resolution sensors remain expensive while affordable low-resolution sensors produce sparse point clouds that miss critical details. LiDAR super-resolution addresses this challenge by using deep learning to enhance sparse point clouds, bridging the gap between different sensor types and enabling cross-sensor compatibility in real-world deployments. This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of LiDAR super-resolution methods for autonomous driving. Despite the importance of practical deployment, no systematic review has been conducted until now. We organize existing approaches into four categories: CNN-based architectures, model-based deep unrolling, implicit representation methods, and Transformer and Mamba-based approaches. We establish fundamental concepts including data representations, problem formulation, benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics. Current trends include the adoption of range image representation for efficient processing, extreme model compression and the development of resolution-flexible architectures. Recent research prioritizes real-time inference and cross-sensor generalization for practical deployment. We conclude by identifying open challenges and future research directions for advancing LiDAR super-resolution technology.

title: Learning human driver dynamics from experiments
authors: Bence Szaksz, Xunbi A. Ji, Tamas G. Molnar, Sergei S. Avedisov, Gábor Stepan, Gábor Orosz
abstract: Human driving dynamics are learned from real field experiments using artificial intelligence (AI), more precisely, using time delay neural networks (TDNNs), which provide a compact way to capture real traffic behavior, up to bistability. The experiments are conducted utilizing the virtual ring concept where an automated vehicle (AV) is driving in front of several human-driven vehicles (HVs), while receiving the position and velocity of the last HV of the chain via wireless vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication. The AV uses this information in its controller to close the virtual ring. It is shown that for certain control parameters, this system exhibits bistable behavior, where it either approaches a steady state or sustained oscillations develop, depending on perturbations. The human driving dynamics is learned by using TDNNs, which capture the nonlinear equation of motion as well as the reaction time delay. We demonstrate that once these networks are substituted into the virtual ring model, bistable behavior develops, confirming the predictive capabilities of the corresponding neural delay differential equation (NDDE). The results support a better understanding of human driving dynamics, which helps in adjusting the control of self-driving vehicles to handle mixed traffic situations.

title: DAVE: Diverse Atomic Visual Elements Dataset with High Representation of Vulnerable Road Users in Complex and Unpredictable Environments
authors: Xijun Wang, Pedro Sandoval-Segura, Chengyuan Zhang, Junyun Huang, Tianrui Guan, Ruiqi Xian, Fuxiao Liu, Rohan Chandra, Boqing Gong, Dinesh Manocha
abstract: Most existing traffic video datasets, such as Waymo [42], are collected in Western countries featuring structured and predictable traffic. In contrast, Asian scenarios are far denser, more unstructured, and heterogeneous, with many agents disobeying traffic rules. Consequently, perception models trained on existing datasets often fail to generalize. To address this, we introduce DAVE, a manually annotated dataset emphasizing Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs) — including pedestrians, animals, motorbikes, and bicycles — in complex, real-world environments. DAVE covers 16 actor categories and 16 action types (e.g., cutins, zigzag movement, U-turns), totaling 13M bounding boxes, of which 1.6M include both actor and action annotations. The videos span diverse weather, lighting, and traffic conditions. DAVE enables benchmarking across multiple video tasks: tracking, detection, spatiotemporal action localization, language-visual moment retrieval, and multi-label video action recognition. VRUs account for 41.13% of instances, compared to 23.14% in Waymo. We also propose DAVE-DETR, a transformer-based detector achieving state-of-the-art performance on DAVE. Overall, DAVE offers a comprehensive, high-complexity benchmark for advancing perception in dense, unpredictable traffic, revealing significant performance degradation in existing methods and promoting progress in robust video understanding.

title: VLM Re-training Framework for Socially-Aware Planning under Dense Urban ODD
authors: Chi-Sheng Shih, Yik Ming Chin, Hsiang-Jui Lin
abstract: Many autonomous driving systems malfunction in dense urban environments where social interactions and uncertainty dominate. Existing approaches rely on either static rule-based modules or learning-based models optimized on scene geometry, and often fail to capture social awareness and contextual reasoning. A socially-informed planner should reason jointly over spatial, semantic, and behavioral cues to generate trajectories aligned with implicit social norms. Toward this goal, this work proposes a Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based framework that unifies social attribute understanding and trajectory generation by fine-tuning pre-trained VLM networks. Leveraging visual inputs and fine-grained action annotations, the models are re-trained with a customized loss function that accounts for trajectory and semantic alignment. Evaluated on a dense urban dataset, the re-trained models show substantial gains across key metrics, including increasing BLEU-4 by 7× (from 0.03 to 0.21) and reducing the L2 distance error by half.

title: A Collaborative Safety Shield for Safe and Efficient CAV Lane Changes in Congested On-Ramp Merging
authors: Bharathkumar Hegde, Mélanie Bouroche
abstract: Lane changing in dense traffic is a significant challenge for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs). Existing lane change controllers primarily either ensure safety or collaboratively improve traffic efficiency, but do not consider these conflicting objectives together. To address this, we propose the Multi-Agent Safety Shield (MASS), designed using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to enable safe and collaborative lane changes. The MASS enables collaboration by capturing multi-agent interactions among CAVs through interaction topologies constructed as a graph using a simple algorithm. Further, a state-of-the-art Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) lane change controller is extended by integrating MASS to ensure safety and defining a customised reward function to prioritise efficiency improvements. As a result, we propose a lane change controller, known as MARL-MASS, and evaluate it in a congested on-ramp merging simulation. The results demonstrate that MASS enables collaborative lane changes with safety guarantees by strictly respecting the safety constraints. Moreover, the proposed custom reward function improves the stability of MARL policies trained with a safety shield. Overall, by encouraging the exploration of a collaborative lane change policy while respecting safety constraints, MARL-MASS effectively balances the tradeoff between ensuring safety and improving traffic efficiency in congested traffic.

title: A Simulation-based Benchmark for LiDAR SLAM in featureless Tunnels with a novel Robustness Evaluation
authors: Qiuyi Cao, Stephanie Grubmüller, Berin Dikic, Selim Solmaz, Robert Wenighofer, Pamela Innerwinkler, Haris Sikic, Eduardo E. Veas
abstract: Numerous LiDAR-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms have been developed for structured indoor and urban environments over the last decades. The applicability to large-scale, GNSS-denied, and featureless environments remains insufficiently investigated. Competitions like the DARPA Subterranean (SubT) Challenge have highlighted the need for reliable SLAM solutions in challenging environments. This paper evaluates whether open-source SLAM algorithms can effectively address these challenges. A high-fidelity simulation of the Zentrum am Berg (ZaB) tunnel facilities in Austria is leveraged to benchmark specific open-source LiDAR-based SLAM algorithms and conduct a robustness evaluation by varying robot motion dynamics, sensor configurations, and environmental feature density. Results show that with appropriate motion and sensor settings, open-source SLAM can achieve reliable performance in large-scale, GNSS-denied, featureless environments.

title: ForestSim: A Synthetic Benchmark for Intelligent Vehicle Perception in Unstructured Forest Environments
authors: Pragat Wagle, Zheng Chen, Lantao Liu
abstract: Robust scene understanding is essential for intelligent vehicles operating in natural, unstructured environments. While semantic segmentation datasets for structured urban driving are abundant, the datasets for extremely unstructured wild environments remain scarce due to the difficulty and cost of generating pixel-accurate annotations. These limitations hinder the development of perception systems needed for intelligent ground vehicles tasked with forestry automation, agricultural robotics, disaster response, and all-terrain mobility. To address this gap, we present ForestSim, a high-fidelity synthetic dataset designed for training and evaluating semantic segmentation models for intelligent vehicles in forested off-road and no-road environments. ForestSim contains 2094 photorealistic images across 25 diverse environments, covering multiple seasons, terrain types, and foliage densities. Using Unreal Engine environments integrated with Microsoft AirSim, we generate consistent, pixel-accurate labels across 20 classes relevant to autonomous navigation. We benchmark ForestSim using state-of-the-art architectures and report strong performance despite the inherent challenges of unstructured scenes. ForestSim provides a scalable and accessible foundation for perception research supporting the next generation of intelligent off-road vehicles. The dataset and code are publicly available:Dataset: https://vailforestsim.github.ioCode: https://github.com/pragatwagle/ForestSim

title: Robust Adaptive Motion Control for Autonomous Vehicle Dynamics under Uncertainties via a Multi-Controller Architecture
authors: Armando Miranda-Moya, Lounis Adouane
abstract: Autonomous vehicle control requires strategies that remain reliable under varying operating conditions. Studies indicate that the behavior of kinematic controllers degrades in moderate and high-speed scenarios. Motivated by this observation, this paper presents a robust and reactive dynamics-based multi-controller architecture for the motion control of an autonomous vehicle subjected to unmatched model and parametric uncertainties. Pose references are processed through a time-varying line-of-sight law to generate heading set-points, whereas a complementary velocity reference is assigned for longitudinal motion. Then, an adaptive integral nonsingular terminal sliding mode controller is formulated to regulate both the heading and velocity states, ensuring practical finite-time convergence, and robustness to disturbances. Closed-loop stability is guaranteed through Lyapunov theory. Simulation results involving a double lane-change and an overtaking maneuver triggered by an elliptic limit-cycle method demonstrate that the proposed framework maintains tracking performance while requiring less control effort and providing smoother control behavior than a kinematics-based nonlinear strategy.

title: A Decision Transformer for Generalizable Multi-Vehicle Coordination at Unsignalized Intersections
authors: Eunjae Lee, Minhee Kang, Yoojin Choi, Heejin Ahn
abstract: We present a Decision Transformer–based approach for coordinating multiple vehicles at unsignalized intersections. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning (RL) or optimization-based methods, our framework formulates coordination as a sequence prediction problem, allowing us to exploit the strengths of Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) architectures. This design enables generating optimal input sequences for multiple vehicles that adapt to diverse scenarios and uncertain traffic dynamics. Extensive experiments show that our approach outperforms traditional offline RL and GPT-based baselines, achieving higher success rates. Furthermore, the model generalizes effectively to unseen layouts and remains robust to perception noise, as validated in both simulation and a real-world miniature testbed.

title: Cooperative automated highway merging evaluation through extensive trials of interoperable prototypes
authors: Joschua Schulte-Tigges, Michele Rondinone, Marcus Kleinehagenbrock, Zinan Liu, Alexander Mödder, Markus Kremer, Michael Reke
abstract: Communication between vehicles can increase automated driving performance and unblock challenging use cases not included in traditional operational design domains (ODDs) like highway merging. Cooperative Maneuvering is a new paradigm by which Connected Automated Vehicles (CAVs) exchange messages to coordinate actions and solve possible driving conflicts earlier and more reliably. Cooperative maneuvering for highway merging has been addressed in a number of simulation studies or demonstrated in small-scale proofs of concept where interacting CAVs share the same implementation. Evaluations with multiple CAVs developed separately by distinct implementers would provide tangible insights on feasibility and performance in real-world scenarios. However, due to their complexity, these evaluations are challenging and time consuming. This paper presents a cooperative automated highway merging assessment based on extensive field trials of CAV prototypes developed by three separate implementers. Detailed descriptions of the key factors ensuring interoperability despite adopting different implementation solutions is given. The methodology for conceptualizing and executing the tests, as well as for deriving results out of collected data is also explained. The assessment compares the cooperative approach with a non-cooperative one and proves advantages in terms of ODD extensions, safety, comfort and traffic efficiency.

title: GTSIGN-220: A Crowd-Sourced, StVO-Aligned Benchmark for Fine-Grained German Traffic Sign Recognition
authors: Miriam Louise Carnot, Erik Fastermann, Jonas Kunze, Eric Peukert, André Ludwig, Bogdan Franczyk
abstract: Robust traffic sign recognition is critical for autonomous driving, intelligent transportation systems, and smart city applications. Multiple datasets for German roads exist, but often fail to capture the full complexity of real-world conditions and regulations. They often lack sufficient class diversity, especially concerning the many additional signs that provide essential contextual information. Synthetic datasets, while scalable, do not fully incorporate all real-world visual effects. To bridge this gap, we present the German Traffic SIGNs (GTSIGN-220) dataset, a new, large-scale benchmark of over 75,000 real-world images across 220 classes. As a key contribution, our dataset was gathered through a nationwide crowdsourcing effort in Germany, ensuring high diversity in camera types, viewpoints, weather conditions, and lighting conditions. It authentically represents in-the-wild challenges such as partial occlusion, motion blur, and vandalism. The inclusion of numerous additional signs enables advanced driver-assistance systems to process nuanced information, such as road damage warnings or specific exemptions. Critically, the dataset’s alignment with the official German Traffic Regulations (StVO) makes it directly applicable for local administrations to automate the inventory and maintenance of their sign databases, bridging the gap between research and practical municipal needs.

title: Landmark-Augmented Multi-Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Shuttle Localization *
authors: Mihai Kocsis, Oliver Knorz, Mike Sautter, Raoul Zöllner
abstract: Reliable and accurate localization is a critical prerequisite for the safe operation of autonomous vehicles, particularly in urban and peri-urban environments where sensor signals are frequently degraded due to multipath effects, occlusions, or limited structural diversity. This paper presents a hybrid localization framework deployed on autonomous shuttles operating in Heilbronn and Bad Wimpfen, Germany. The system integrates high-precision GNSS, LiDAR-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), wheel and inertial odometry and a novel retroreflector-based topological landmark system. All modalities are fused using an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to provide continuous, robust, and interpretable pose estimates suitable for public transport deployment. The paper provides a detailed description of the system architecture, sensor setup, marker-based localization methodology, EKF fusion strategy and experimental validation, obtained from more than 6000 kilometers of autonomous operation.

title: SODBoost: Density-Guided Zoom-In Mosaic for Small Object Detection
authors: Jinlun Yu, Yuehai Chen, Yi Shi, Jing Yang
abstract: Small object detection (SOD) underpins critical applications such as aerial surveillance, autonomous driving and robotics, yet remains inherently challenging due to weak feature representation and unstable optimization. To address these issues, we propose SODBoost, a plug-and-play framework designed to Boost Small Object Detection with two training-only modules. Density-Guided Zoom-In Mosaic targets the problem of weak supervision for small objects by adaptively focusing data augmentation on high-density small object regions, thereby enriching effective supervision without compromising normal-scale performance. Scale-Adaptive Similarity mitigates the instability of IoU-based regression by introducing a scale-aware interpolation between location similarity and GIoU through a gating mechanism, producing smooth and consistent gradients across scales. Integrated into representative real-time DETR-based detectors, extensive experiments on VisDrone benchmark demonstrate that SODBoost consistently enhances small object detection performance while incurring zero inference overhead.

title: Pedestrian Micro-Doppler Signatures: Experimental Analysis with 77 GHz Automotive Radar
authors: Siddharth Murali, Jue Zhou, Yaobin Chen, Stanley Chien, Chi-Chih Chen, Ananna Ahmed, Rini Sherony
abstract: This paper presents the findings of our experimental study of pedestrian micro-Doppler (MD) responses, collected from a commercial-off-the-shelf 77 GHz automotive radar across various pedestrian motion scenarios, including directions, patterns, paces, and distances. Our study aimed to investigate the feasibility of using a commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) 77 GHz automotive radar to obtain MD signatures for pedestrian detection. The preliminary results indicate that this 77 GHz radar can effectively capture pedestrian MD signatures across most motion scenarios at distances and angles relevant to AEB operations. This study has two main contributions: (1) Collected a large dataset of pedestrian radar responses from a COTS 77GHz automotive radar in controlled environments and extracted pedestrian MD responses from COTS radar data. This dataset will enable future pedestrian detection using MD signatures. (2) Confirmed the existence of pedestrian micro-Doppler features from the COTS 77GHz automotive radar output in a distance relevant to the AEB application.

title: REvolve+: Policy-as-Code Evolution for Autonomous Driving
authors: Alkis Sygkounas, Andreas Persson, Amy Loutfi
abstract: Modern autonomous driving systems increasingly depend on large-scale learned controllers, yet their behavior is often opaque and difficult to adjust once deployed. Recent progress in language-model–guided optimization enables control logic to be represented as executable programs that can be directly inspected and evolved, effectively turning policy learning into a form of program evolution. Building upon REvolve, which evolved reward functions through human feedback, this work introduces REvolve+, an extension that evolves executable driving policies represented as source code. To reduce reliance on costly human evaluation and improve interpretability, we replace scalar reward values with analytic driving metrics and automate the discovery of fitness functions via majority voting from a large language model (LLM). In addition, we introduce a Pareto-based multi-objective formulation that jointly optimizes these metrics without fixed weighting aggregation, advancing beyond single-objective fitness optimization. Experiments in the CARLA simulator across multiple environments compare the analytic, LLM-derived, and Pareto-based baselines, including the CARLA autopilot, and show that the multi-objective formulation results in more stable, consistent policy improvement. The results position policy-as-code evolution as an interpretable, fully automated alternative to black-box reinforcement learning for autonomous driving.

title: Pedestrian Crossing Intent Prediction via Psychological Features and Transformer Fusion
authors: Sima Ashayer, Hoang H. Nguyen, Yu Liang, Mina Sartipi
abstract: Pedestrian intention prediction needs to be accurate for autonomous vehicles to navigate safely in urban environments. We present a lightweight, socially informed architecture for pedestrian intention prediction. It fuses four behavioral streams (attention, position, situation, and interaction) using highway encoders, a compact 4-token Transformer, and global self-attention pooling. To quantify uncertainty, we incorporate two complementary heads: a variational bottleneck whose KL divergence captures epistemic uncertainty, and a Mahalanobis distance detector that identifies distributional shift. Together, these components yield calibrated probabilities and actionable risk scores without compromising efficiency. On the PSI 1.0 benchmark, our model outperforms recent vision–language models by achieving 0.9 F1, 0.94 AUC-ROC, and 0.78 MCC by using only structured, interpretable features. On the more diverse PSI 2.0 dataset, where, to the best of our knowledge, no prior results exist, we establish a strong initial baseline of 0.78 F1 and 0.79 AUC-ROC. Selective prediction based on Mahalanobis scores increases test accuracy by up to 0.4 percentage points at 80% coverage. Qualitative attention heatmaps further show how the model shifts its cross-stream focus under ambiguity. The proposed approach is modality-agnostic, easy to integrate with vision–language pipelines, and suitable for risk-aware intent prediction on resource-constrained platforms.
